title: Insulation
short_answer: Trap still air — fill every cavity completely and never compress the batt. Gaps and compression are the only two ways to fail, and both are invisible an hour later.
summary: The fastest trade in this manual to install badly in a way nobody can see. It gets covered the same day, and it either performs or it doesn't.
plain_words: Insulation works by trapping still air. That means it has to fill the cavity completely and it must not be squashed. Cut batts to fit snug — a batt jammed in behind a pipe or stuffed short at the top is doing a fraction of its job. Gaps and compression are the only two ways to get this wrong, and they're both invisible an hour later.
when_to_use: MEP rough-in complete and inspected; before the second side of board goes on
Thermal batts in exterior walls and anywhere an R-value is specified
Sound attenuation batts (SAB) in partitions with STC requirements
Fire safing at slab edges, shafts, and rated penetrations per listed assembly
prerequisites: MEP rough-in complete and inspected in the cavity
Wall type schedule identifies batt type, facing, and R-value or STC
Fire safing material and listed assembly identified when safing is in scope

tools.name: Utility knife and spare blades for batt cutting
Staple gun for faced batt flanges (when spec requires)
Long sleeves, gloves, and eye protection
Respirator per manufacturer guidance and GVC program

materials.name: Thermal batt (faced or unfaced per schedule)
Sound attenuation batt (SAB) for STC partitions
Rigid board insulation for Z-furring and slab edges
Mineral wool fire safing per listed assembly
Acoustic sealant at perimeter and penetrations (when detail requires)

steps.body: Only after MEP rough-in is complete and inspected, and before the second side of board goes on.
Friction fit — cut slightly wide of the cavity so it holds itself, then let it relax to full thickness.
Fill the cavity top to bottom. If the wall runs to deck, the insulation runs to deck — including the part above the ceiling nobody will ever look at.
Never compress to get around something. At pipes and conduit, split the batt and pass half behind and half in front. Compressing in front of a pipe leaves a cold, loud void behind it.
At electrical boxes, cut the batt to fit around the box, not squash against it.
Cut narrow cavities to fit rather than folding a full-width batt into them.
On faced batts, confirm the facing direction from the drawings and staple the flanges without compressing the batt.
Don't leave batts sagging or falling out ahead of the board crew — support them if there's any delay.
Every cavity full, top to bottom, no gaps at the track.
No compression anywhere — especially behind pipe, conduit, and boxes.
Correct type in the correct wall, and facing the correct direction.
Sound walls: perimeter and penetrations sealed per the detail.
To-deck walls insulated above the ceiling line.
Safing installed as the listed assembly requires, and photographed.
Photos of insulated walls by room before they're closed.

warnings.title: Why care when nobody will ever see it
warnings.body: The two things insulation is usually there for are energy bills and sound. A sound wall with a two-inch gap at the top of every cavity is not a sound wall — the complaint arrives after the building is occupied, when opening the wall costs a hundred times what filling the gap would have.

warnings.title: Safing is not the same as insulation
warnings.body: Fire safing looks like insulation and isn't. It's a rated component in a listed assembly, with specified material, density, thickness, and compression. Substituting a thermal batt for mineral wool safing, or packing it loose, is a rated-assembly failure, not an insulation shortcut. See Firestopping.

experts.summary: An STC rating belongs to the whole assembly, not the insulation. Board layers, stud type and spacing, whether the wall runs to deck, and whether the assembly is sealed all matter as much as the batt. Seal the perimeter with acoustic sealant where the detail calls for it; seal penetrations at boxes, sleeves, and conduit; offset back-to-back electrical boxes on sound walls. A partition stopped at a suspended ceiling with an open plenum transmits over the top — if drawings show STC and the wall stops at the ceiling, ask the question. Full-height insulation above the ceiling line on to-deck walls is not optional detail work — it's what makes the rating real.

variations.title: Thermal batt
variations.when: Exterior walls and anywhere an R-value is specified
changes: Faced or unfaced per schedule — confirm facing direction from drawings
Friction fit full cavity height including above ceiling on to-deck walls

variations.title: Sound attenuation batt (SAB)
variations.when: Interior partitions with STC — offices, exam rooms, restrooms, corridors
changes: Usually unfaced; full height matters more than anything else
Perimeter and penetration sealing per acoustic detail

variations.title: Rigid board
variations.when: Behind Z-furring on masonry, slab edges, under some assemblies
changes: Cut tight between furring — see Metal Stud Framing Z-furring guidance

variations.title: Fire safing
variations.when: Slab edges, shafts, and rated penetrations
changes: Mineral wool per listed assembly — not interchangeable with thermal batt

quality_checks.prompt: Every cavity full top to bottom with no gaps at track
No compression behind pipes, conduit, or boxes
Correct batt type, facing direction, and wall assignment
Sound walls: perimeter and penetrations sealed per detail
Insulated walls photographed by room before board closes

common_mistakes.title: Gap at top of cavity
common_mistakes.wrong: Batt stuffed short or missing above ceiling line
common_mistakes.right: Full height to deck on to-deck walls
common_mistakes.why: Sound and thermal performance fail invisible until occupied

common_mistakes.title: Compressing around pipe
common_mistakes.wrong: Jam full batt in front of pipe or conduit
common_mistakes.right: Split batt — half behind, half in front
common_mistakes.why: Cold and loud void behind the obstruction

common_mistakes.title: Squashing at electrical box
common_mistakes.right: Cut batt to fit around box

common_mistakes.title: Wrong facing direction
common_mistakes.wrong: Install faced batt without checking drawings
common_mistakes.right: Confirm vapor retarder orientation from spec and climate
common_mistakes.why: Moisture and warranty issues — never a field guess

common_mistakes.title: Thermal batt for fire safing
common_mistakes.wrong: Substitute fiberglass batt at slab edge or shaft
common_mistakes.right: Mineral wool per listed assembly; photograph
common_mistakes.why: Rated assembly failure, not an insulation shortcut

common_mistakes.title: Sound wall with open plenum
common_mistakes.wrong: Insulate partition that stops at ceiling without asking
common_mistakes.right: Ask when STC is specified and wall doesn't run to deck
common_mistakes.why: Sound flanks over the ceiling — batt below cannot fix it

common_mistakes.title: Sagging batts before board
common_mistakes.wrong: Leave batts unsupported while waiting for board crew
common_mistakes.why: Falls out or compresses before close

provenance.note: Friction fit, full-cavity coverage, splitting batts around obstructions, and avoiding compression follow standard manufacturer installation guidance — trapped still air is the physics. R-values, STC ratings, facing and vapor retarder direction, and safing materials are project-specific from the wall type schedule, specification, and listed assembly. Vapor retarder orientation depends on climate zone and assembly design and should never be decided in the field. Safing requirements come from the listed firestop assembly, not from this page.
